Decentralized Dynamic Stable Matching

Jing Chen    Mengtong Gao    Zhenhe Zhang Email: jchencs@tsinghua.edu.cn Affiliation: {gmt25, zhenhe-z21}@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Technology Affiliation: Tsinghua University, Beijing, China
Abstract

In this work we study decentralized computing of the player-optimal stable matching (POSM) under unannounced player arrivals and departures. Without a common clock, arrival/departure events information, or direct communication, players can only make individual proposals to the arms and observe individual accept/reject outcomes. We measure the mismatch cost — the total number of rounds in which the realized matching differs from the POSM of that round, as the time horizon TT grows. For known preferences, we develop a deterministic polynomial-time self-calibrating protocol that achieves a mismatch cost of O⁡(t∗+K2​log⁡T)O(t_{*}+K^{2}\log T), greatly improving the existing upper-bound O⁡(T1−1/K​(log⁡T)2/K)O(T^{1-1/K}(\log T)^{2/K}). Here KK and t∗t_{*} are respectively the number of arms and the time of the last event in the problem instance. Each player individually runs the protocol based on his/her own local time and proposal-outcome history, without knowing t∗t_{*} or TT. More generally, our protocol can be configured with a non-decreasing and polynomial-time-computable function g⁡(t)=Ω⁡(t)g(t)=\Omega(t), so as to achieve a mismatch cost of O⁡(g⁡(t∗)+K2​Ng​(T))O(g(t_{*})+K^{2}N_{g}(T)), where Ng​(T)N_{g}(T) counts iterations of t↦t+g⁡(t)t\mapsto t+g(t) below TT. Roughly speaking, g⁡(t)g(t) reflects the protocol’s convergence speed. The relationship between g⁡(t)g(t) and Ng​(T)N_{g}(T) highlights the tradeoff between convergence speed and asymptotic mismatch cost.

We next show that any randomized protocol with a convergence speed g⁡(t)≥1g(t)\geq 1 and an asymptotic sublinear mismatch cost has a worst-case expected cost of Ω⁡(t∗+Ng​(T))\Omega(t_{*}+N_{g}(T)). This further implies that, up to a K2K^{2} factor, our protocol with g⁡(t)=tg(t)=t is optimal among all protocols with sublinear cost and convergence speed O⁡(t∗)O(t_{*}). Finally, for unknown preferences on both sides, each player and each arm individually observe their own preferences after being matched to the other side. We develop a decentralized learning protocol that achieves expected mismatch cost O⁡(t∗+K4​Δmin−2​log⁡T)O(t_{*}+K^{4}\Delta_{\mathrm{min}}^{-2}\log T), where Δmin\Delta_{\mathrm{min}} measures the preference gaps in the learning problem. A complementary static-setting lower bound adapted from the literature establishes that the dependencies on TT and Δmin\Delta_{\mathrm{min}} are tight.

Keywords: stable matching; decentralized algorithm; dynamic matching market; multi-arm bandit.

1 Introduction

Classical studies of two-sided matching markets focus on computing a stable matching for a fixed set of participants. When preferences are known, player-proposing deferred acceptance (DA) computes the player-optimal stable matching (POSM), which assigns to each player its most preferred arm among all stable matchings [GS62]. In dynamic markets, player arrivals and departures may change the POSM. Without any notification of these changes, remaining players may continue being matched to their previously assigned arms, even when the resulting matching is no longer the current POSM. In this work, we study decentralized protocols for maintaining the POSM under such changes, where each player acts on its own local clock and proposal-outcome history. We measure the cumulative mismatch cost by the number of rounds in which the realized matching differs from the POSM of that round, as the time horizon TT grows.

As a toy example, consider two players p,qp,q and two arms a,ba,b. Both players prefer aa to bb, arm aa prefers pp to qq, and arm bb prefers qq to pp. With both players present, the POSM assigns pp to aa and qq to bb. If pp departs, the new POSM should have assigned qq to aa, but player qq continues to be accepted when proposing to bb. In fact, as long as qq continues proposing to bb, it receives the same acceptance outcome whether pp stays or departs. To distinguish the two cases, therefore, qq must propose to aa, which disrupts the correct matching if pp is still present. This creates a trade-off between recovery from hidden departures and maintenance of a correct matching in a static scenario where the population doesn’t change.

Besides detecting population changes, players must also coordinate in a decentralized manner when computing the POSM. They may have different arrival times and local states, without a common clock, population roster, or direct communication. Consequently, coordination must be achieved through individual proposals and accept/reject outcomes. To tackle these problems, our approach alternates between deferred acceptance and replay of the resulting matching, using only a player’s local information to schedule subsequent computation.

1.1 Our Contributions

Dynamic matching with known preferences.

We develop Self-Calibrating Deferred Acceptance (SC-DA), a deterministic decentralized protocol for maintaining the POSM when preferences are known. With KK arms and finitely many player arrivals and departures, SC-DA achieves cumulative mismatch cost O⁡(t∗+K2​log⁡T)O(t_{*}+K^{2}\log T), where TT is the time horizon and t∗t_{*} is the last population-event time. Using only each player’s local clock and proposal-outcome history, the protocol coordinates deferred acceptance computations and calibrates replay lengths without requiring any player to know TT or t∗t_{*}.

Recovery–mismatch trade-off.

More generally, SC-DA can be configured with a recovery scale function gg, yielding different guarantees on convergence speed and asymptotic mismatch cost. We establish an information-theoretic lower bound on the cost of maintaining the POSM. Any protocol with sublinear mismatch cost relative to gg incurs Ω​(Ng​(T))\Omega(N_{g}(T)) expected cumulative mismatch in the worst case, even when the market remains static. For the linear choice g⁡(t)=tg(t)=t, our dynamic lower bound further establishes the asymptotic optimality of SC-DA up to a factor K2K^{2}.

Dynamic matching with two-sided learning.

We develop Self-Calibrating Preference Certification (SC-PC), a decentralized protocol for maintaining the POSM when both players and arms must learn their preferences. SC-PC achieves expected cumulative mismatch O⁡(t∗+K4​Δmin−2​log⁡T)O(t_{*}+K^{4}\Delta_{\min}^{-2}\log T), where Δmin\Delta_{\mathrm{min}} denotes the minimum relevant preference gap in the final market, as defined in Section 5.1. A lower bound adapted from prior work shows that the dependence on TT and Δmin\Delta_{\min} is tight even in static markets.

1.2 Related Work

Dynamic matching markets.

Dynamic matching has been studied under evolving preferences and rewards, with objectives including the number of blocking pairs, changes between stable matchings, and nonstationary regret [KLM16, BCK+20, GSR+24, MMKS23]. Closest to our setting, [GZL+26] study decentralized matching bandits with unannounced player arrivals and departures and no global clock. The Way-SE-2S algorithm uses a Restless Ping mechanism to probe arms that may become attainable following hidden departures and achieves per-player POSM regret with horizon dependence O⁡(T1−1/K​(log⁡T)2/K)O(T^{1-1/K}(\log T)^{2/K}) under two-sided learning. Building on this setting, we isolate the coordination and recovery challenges caused by population changes from preference learning, and develop a self-calibrating mechanism that addresses these challenges with POSM mismatch in the known-preference setting and extends to two-sided learning.

Recovery and maintenance in distributed protocols.

A central question in distributed computing is how quickly correctness can be restored after changes and how long it can be maintained. Dynamic size-counting protocols study convergence and holding times under adversarial population changes [DE22, KL24], while loosely-stabilizing leader election establishes a tight trade-off between these times [SEIM21]. For matching, self-stabilizing stable-marriage algorithms recover stable matchings from arbitrary configurations [LMB+17, BBB+18], and dynamic maximal-matching algorithms bound cumulative incorrect rounds with topology-change notifications and message passing [CHDK+21]. Silent-failure monitoring separately studies the trade-off between probing overhead and detection delay [CHK+14]. In our setting, departures are unannounced, and detecting them requires proposals that may disrupt the POSM even when the market remains static, directly coupling recovery requirements with cumulative mismatch.

Learning in matching markets.

Bandit matching markets study preference learning through repeated interactions [LMJ20]. For player-side learning in static markets, decentralized approaches differ in their feedback and coordination mechanisms, including publicly observed matching outcomes [LRMJ21, KL23, KWL24], phase-based exploration [BSS21], and deliberate collision-based communication [ZWF22]. Coordination-free learning has been studied under structural assumptions on preferences [MSM22] and through game-theoretic dynamics [ES25]. For two-sided preference learning, existing methods employ player indexing and coordinated exploration [PG24, ZF24], or use super-stability to certify stable matchings from partial preference rankings [Bas25]. Completely uncoupled trial-and-error learning has also been studied with noiseless utility feedback [SFM25]. Our work combines two-sided preference learning with unannounced player arrivals and departures, using local feedback to maintain the current POSM while controlling cumulative mismatch.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Dynamic Market and Stable Matchings

We consider a dynamic two-sided matching market with K≥2K\geq 2 fixed arms, indexed by 𝒦={0,…,K−1}\mathcal{K}=\{0,\ldots,K-1\}, where KK is publicly known. Time proceeds in discrete rounds t=1,2,…t=1,2,\ldots. Each player ii enters at round bi≥1b_{i}\geq 1 and departs at round di>bid_{i}>b_{i}, with di=∞d_{i}=\infty if the player never leaves. The set of active players at round tt is 𝒫t={i:bi≤t<di}\mathcal{P}_{t}=\{i:b_{i}\leq t<d_{i}\}, and |𝒫t|≤K|\mathcal{P}_{t}|\leq K for all tt. We consider markets with finitely many player arrivals and departures. Counting the initial market as a population event in round 11, we denote the last population-event time by t∗t_{*}.

Both sides have complete, strict preference rankings over the other side, represented by fixed true utilities. For each player ii, the utility of arm kk is μi,k∈[0,1]\mu_{i,k}\in[0,1]; for each arm kk, the utility of player ii is πk,i∈[0,1]\pi_{k,i}\in[0,1]. Their preferences satisfy

k≻iℓ⇔μi,k>μi,ℓ,i≻kj⇔πk,i>πk,j.k\succ_{i}\ell\iff\mu_{i,k}>\mu_{i,\ell},\qquad i\succ_{k}j\iff\pi_{k,i}>\pi_{k,j}.

All agents prefer any partner to remaining unmatched. We write ranki⁡(k)\operatorname{rank}_{i}(k) and rankk⁡(i)\operatorname{rank}_{k}(i) for the corresponding preference ranks, with rank 11 being the most preferred. Let pi​(r)p_{i}(r) denote player ii’s arm of rank rr. Each arm’s ranking is defined over all players that participate at any time in the instance.

At each round tt, a matching mm consists of disjoint player–arm pairs from 𝒫t×𝒦\mathcal{P}_{t}\times\mathcal{K}. We write m⁡(i)m(i) for player ii’s assigned arm, with m(i)=⊥m(i)=\bot when ii is unmatched. A pair (i,k)(i,k) is a blocking pair of mm if player ii and arm kk prefer each other to their respective partners under mm. A matching is stable if all active players are matched and no blocking pair exists.

Among all stable matchings at round tt, the POSM, denoted by mt∗m_{t}^{*}, assigns each active player its most preferred arm attainable in any stable matching:

μi,mt∗​(i)≥μi,m⁡(i)for every stable matching ​m​ and every ​i∈𝒫t.\mu_{i,m_{t}^{*}(i)}\geq\mu_{i,m(i)}\quad\text{for every stable matching }m\text{ and every }i\in\mathcal{P}_{t}.

The POSM is unique and can be computed by player-proposing deferred acceptance [GS62].

2.2 Decentralized Protocol Model

A decentralized protocol specifies how players make proposals and how arms respond, using only locally available information. In each round tt, every active player proposes to exactly one arm. Each arm observes its proposers and accepts one if the proposal set is nonempty; all other proposers are rejected. The accepted player–arm pairs form the realized matching MtM_{t}.

Upon entry, player ii initializes its local state and sets its local clock to 00. Its local age in round tt is ai=t−bia_{i}=t-b_{i}. Active players retain their local states across population changes. Each player observes whether its proposal is accepted or rejected (A/R) and, when accepted, its realized utility. Neither players nor arms have access to a global clock. Players cannot observe the active player set 𝒫t\mathcal{P}_{t} or other players’ actions and feedback. No direct communication, population-event notification, or public reset is available.

In the known-preference setting, each player ii knows its true utilities {μi,k}k∈𝒦\{\mu_{i,k}\}_{k\in\mathcal{K}}, and each arm knows its true utilities {πk,i}i\{\pi_{k,i}\}_{i}. Each arm accepts its highest-ranked current proposer; the rule uses no interaction history.

In the two-sided learning setting, both players and arms initially lack knowledge of their own true utilities and preference rankings. When player ii is matched with arm kk, both sides observe their respective stochastic utilities in [0,1][0,1]. Conditional on the complete interaction history and the current proposals and acceptance decisions, their expected utilities are μi,k\mu_{i,k} and πk,i\pi_{k,i}, respectively. Rejected proposals yield no utility observations. Each arm recognizes returning proposers through private handles with a fixed local ordering and maintains its own local clock and interaction history. Its acceptance decisions may depend on these records.

2.3 Tracking Objective and Performance Measure

An instance II specifies both sides’ true utilities and a population path fixed independently of the protocol’s randomization and utility observations. In the two-sided learning setting, II also specifies the conditional distributions of utility observations, subject to the assumptions above.

For a protocol Π\Pi and an integer time horizon T≥1T\geq 1, we define the cumulative POSM mismatch cost as

DΠ(T;I)=∑t=1T𝟏{Mt≠mt∗}.D_{\Pi}(T;I)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf{1}\{M_{t}\neq m_{t}^{*}\}. (1)

We write D⁡(T,I)D(T;I) when the protocol is clear. This cost counts rounds in which the realized matching differs from the POSM of that round, whereas binary stable regret [Bas25] counts rounds in which the matching is not stable.

When utility observations or protocol decisions are random, we consider the expected mismatch cost 𝔼​[DΠ​(T,I)]\mathbb{E}[D_{\Pi}(T;I)]. The protocol’s decision rules are fixed before the instance and horizon are chosen; agents are not given TT or t∗t_{*}.

3 Dynamic Matching with Known Preferences

After a population change, players that remain active may continue to be accepted by their previously assigned arms even when the resulting matching is no longer the current POSM. We introduce Self-Calibrating Deferred Acceptance (SC-DA), which combines coordinated computation of the POSM via deferred acceptance with replay of the resulting matching. Each player calibrates its replay length using its own local clock, enabling recovery from unannounced population changes while limiting cumulative mismatch.

3.1 The Self-Calibrating Deferred Acceptance Protocol

To compute the POSM, SC-DA coordinates players with different arrival times and local states. Priority competition at a designated arm allows one player to initiate a sweep across all arms. In a fixed market, a successful sweep initiates a coordinated computation of the POSM using player-proposing deferred acceptance. Since the computation phase has the same duration for every player, the offsets between their entry times into this phase are preserved at completion.

After computation, each player saves its output arm and repeatedly proposes to it until a rejection or its replay deadline triggers another coordination attempt. Subsequent computations are scheduled through self-calibration. Each player uses its own clock and the age recorded at its preceding computation output to count the rounds since that output and set its next replay length.

SC-DA uses four player-local modes: Replay, Seek, Sweep, and Work. In Replay, a player repeatedly proposes to its saved arm. Seek and Sweep coordinate active players for the next computation, while Work performs the matching computation and updates the replay length and deadlines. Each newly arriving player starts in Seek. Figure 1 illustrates the state transitions, and Algorithm 1 specifies the player-local rules.

We designate arm 00 as BUS for coordinating players and arm 11 as PARK for the initial stage of matching computation. For each player ii, let TOPi=pi​(1)\mathrm{TOP}_{i}=p_{i}(1) denote its most preferred arm. The protocol sets

J=K2+5​K+1,H=4​J+4.J=K^{2}+5K+1,\qquad H=4J+4. (2)

Here JJ determines the duration of Work and the number of consecutive BUS acceptances required to enter Sweep, while HH specifies the minimum replay length.

Replay.

In Replay, a player repeatedly proposes to its saved arm yy. A rejection causes it to enter Seek in the next round, whereas reaching its replay deadline qq causes it to enter Seek at the start of that round (Lines 22–23 and 13–14, respectively, in Algorithm 1). The deadline ensures periodic computation even when the player continues to be accepted by its current arm.

Seek.

A player in Seek repeatedly proposes to BUS. In a fixed market, we call the active player most preferred by BUS the root. Priority competition at BUS allows the root to accumulate consecutive acceptances and eventually enter Sweep.

Each player maintains a counter ρ\rho, initially zero and capped at JJ, recording consecutive BUS acceptances. An accepted BUS proposal increments ρ\rho up to JJ, while a BUS rejection or a proposal to another arm resets it to zero. The counter is updated in every mode and preserved across mode transitions. (Lines 21 of Algorithm 1). At the start of a round, a player in Seek with ρ=J\rho=J enters Sweep (Lines 16–17 of Algorithm 1).

On entering Seek, a player clears its rejection flag, which is set upon receiving a BUS rejection. Once the flag is set, two consecutive BUS acceptances trigger an AA handoff, and the player enters Work in the following round (Lines 24–27 of Algorithm 1).

Sweep.

A player entering Sweep repeatedly executes 2​K2K-round blocks, each with the proposal sequence

σ=(0,1,0,2,…,0,K−1,0,0).\sigma=(0,1,0,2,\ldots,0,K-1,0,0). (3)

A rejection at BUS causes the player to return to Seek in the next round. A rejection at a non-BUS arm marks the current block as unsuccessful; the player completes the block and starts a new one unless rejected at BUS. If every proposal in a block is accepted, the player enters Work in the following round (see SweepFeedback, called in Line 29 of Algorithm 1).

The sweep visits every arm while leaving BUS for only one round at a time. A successful block also brings players in Replay back to Seek, preparing them for the next coordinated computation.

Work.

A player enters Work following either an AA handoff or a successful sweep. Each Work invocation lasts exactly JJ rounds and consists of three consecutive stages: Park, Top, and DA (see SelectArm in Algorithm 1).

In Park, the player proposes to PARK for 2​K2K rounds, leaving BUS available for other players to enter Work. In Top, it proposes to its first-choice arm TOPi\mathrm{TOP}_{i} for the next 2​K+12K+1 rounds. When players enter Work at staggered two-round offsets, their Top stages share a round in which all players propose to their first-choice arms.

In DA, the player uses an application index kk, initially 11, to propose to arm pi​(k)p_{i}(k) for the remaining J−4​K−1J-4K-1 rounds. Upon acceptance, it continues proposing to the same arm. After a rejection in a nonfinal DA round, it increases kk by one, capped at KK (Lines 36–37 of Algorithm 1). These repeated proposals implement the application and rejection steps of deferred acceptance.

In the final Work round, regardless of the feedback, the player records its proposed arm as the computation output yy and updates

L=H+2​(a−ℓ),q=a+L,ℓ←a,L=H+2(a-\ell),\qquad q=a+L,\qquad\ell\leftarrow a, (4)

where aa is its current local age and ℓ\ell is the age of its preceding Work completion, initially zero. The update uses the previous value of ℓ\ell. The player enters Replay in the following round (Lines 32–34 of Algorithm 1). Section 3.2 establishes the performance guarantees and extends the analysis to more general convergence speeds.

3.2 Performance Upper Bounds

We first establish the cumulative mismatch guarantee of SC-DA under known preferences.

Theorem 1 (Cumulative Mismatch of SC-DA).

For every K≥2K\geq 2, every legal finite-event instance II in the known-preference setting with last population-event time t∗t_{*}, and every T≥1T\geq 1, SC-DA satisfies

D⁡(T,I)=O⁡(t∗+K2​log⁡T).D(T;I)=O(t_{*}+K^{2}\log T).

In a fixed nonempty market, suppose that two coordinated computations give consecutive actual outputs to every player, with each player’s output offset from the root unchanged between the two computations. Let o1<o2o_{1}<o_{2} be the root’s output rounds and let δi\delta_{i} be player ii’s common output offset in the two computations. Let ai′a_{i}^{\prime} and aia_{i} denote player ii’s local ages at the first and second outputs, respectively. Using its entry round bib_{i}, we have

ai′\displaystyle a_{i}^{\prime} =o1+δi−bi,ai=o2+δi−bi,\displaystyle=o_{1}+\delta_{i}-b_{i},\qquad a_{i}=o_{2}+\delta_{i}-b_{i},
ai−ai′\displaystyle a_{i}-a_{i}^{\prime} =(o2+δi−bi)−(o1+δi−bi)=o2−o1.\displaystyle=(o_{2}+\delta_{i}-b_{i})-(o_{1}+\delta_{i}-b_{i})=o_{2}-o_{1}.

Thus the elapsed time between the two outputs is the same for every player. Since the outputs are consecutive in each player’s actual history, the old register satisfies ℓi=ai′\ell_{i}=a_{i}^{\prime} at the second output. The replay update in (4) therefore gives all players the same replay length using only their local output histories.

The same equality of replay lengths holds when all players apply a common function to a−ℓa-\ell. More generally, let g:ℕ≥1→ℕ≥1g:\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}\to\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1} be nondecreasing and polynomial-time computable with g⁡(t)=Ω⁡(t)g(t)=\Omega(t). Here gg specifies the desired convergence speed. Define

s0\displaystyle s_{0} =H,sj+1=sj+g(sj)(j≥0),\displaystyle=H,\qquad s_{j+1}=s_{j}+g(s_{j})\quad(j\geq 0), (5)
Fg​(x)\displaystyle F_{g}(x) =H+2x+max({g(sj)−sj:j≥0, 64sj≤x}∪{0}),x≥1.\displaystyle=H+2x+\max\Bigl(\{g(s_{j})-s_{j}:j\geq 0,\ 64s_{j}\leq x\}\cup\{0\}\Bigr),\qquad x\geq 1.

Define Πg\Pi_{g} by replacing only the replay-length assignment in (4) and Line 33 in Algorithm 1 with L←Fg​(a−ℓ)L\leftarrow F_{g}(a-\ell). When g⁡(t)=tg(t)=t, we have Fg​(x)=H+2​xF_{g}(x)=H+2x, so Πg\Pi_{g} coincides with SC-DA.

The next two lemmas connect the calibration identity to the protocol’s execution. Lemma 1 guarantees the two computations needed for calibration. To state its recovery bound, define ΨFg​(x)=x+Fg​(x+H)+3​H\Psi_{F_{g}}(x)=x+F_{g}(x+H)+3H. Lemma 2 then shows that subsequent maintenance preserves calibration. Their proofs appear in Appendices A.4 and A.5, respectively.

Lemma 1 (Recovery and Calibration).

For every legal finite-event instance II with last population-event time t∗t_{*} and a nonempty final market, Πg\Pi_{g} produces two coordinated computations of the final POSM, both initiated after t∗t_{*}. Each player’s outputs are consecutive in its actual output history and have the same offset from the root’s output in both computations. Let VcalV_{\mathrm{cal}} be the round when all active players have entered Replay after the second computation. At this round, their replay lengths agree and the realized matching equals the final POSM, with

t∗<Vcal≤ΨFg∘3​(t∗+1).t_{*}<V_{\mathrm{cal}}\leq\Psi_{F_{g}}^{\circ 3}(t_{*}+1).

The players’ global replay deadlines retain the output offsets because their replay lengths agree. After this calibration, a maintenance window begins at the root’s replay deadline and ends when all active players have returned to Replay after the next computation.

Lemma 2 (Maintenance after Calibration).

Starting from the calibration in Lemma 1, each maintenance window of Πg\Pi_{g} produces every player’s next actual output in a coordinated computation of the final POSM, preserving the fixed output offsets and a common replay length. The matching equals the final POSM outside these windows, each lasting O⁡(K2)O(K^{2}) rounds uniformly over gg and II. The common replay lengths L0,L1,…L_{0},L_{1},\ldots, starting with the calibrated length L0L_{0}, satisfy

L0≥H,Lj+1≥Fg(Lj)(j≥0).L_{0}\geq H,\qquad L_{j+1}\geq F_{g}(L_{j})\qquad(j\geq 0).

To bound the number of maintenance windows, define

r0=2,rj+1=rj+g⁡(rj),Ng​(T)=#⁡{j≥0:rj<T}.r_{0}=2,\qquad r_{j+1}=r_{j}+g(r_{j}),\qquad N_{g}(T)=\#\{j\geq 0:r_{j}<T\}. (6)
Lemma 3 (Properties of the Replay Rule FgF_{g}).

4 Lower Bounds and Optimality

Detecting an unannounced departure may require proposals that disrupt an otherwise correct matching. We formalize the resulting recovery requirement, establish the necessary mismatch cost, and characterize optimal static maintenance. Throughout this section, we consider the known-preference setting, where each arm accepts its most preferred proposer in every round.

4.1 Recovery and Necessary Mismatch

For a protocol Π\Pi and a legal finite-event instance II with last population-event time t∗t_{*}, define

LΠ​(h,I)=𝔼⁡[DΠ​(t∗+h,I)−DΠ​(t∗,I)],h≥1.L_{\Pi}(h;I)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[D_{\Pi}(t_{*}+h;I)-D_{\Pi}(t_{*};I)\right],\qquad h\geq 1. (8)

This is the expected mismatch in rounds t∗+1,…,t∗+ht_{*}+1,\ldots,t_{*}+h, after the last population event. Players that remain active across the event retain their actual states.

Definition 1 (Sublinear mismatch cost relative to gg).

Let g:ℕ≥1→ℕ≥1g:\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}\to\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1} be nondecreasing. A decentralized matching protocol Π\Pi has sublinear mismatch cost relative to gg if, for every ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), there is a constant cε>0c_{\varepsilon}>0 such that, for every legal finite-event instance II with last population-event time t∗t_{*} and every h≥cε​g​(t∗)h\geq c_{\varepsilon}g(t_{*}),

LΠ​(h,I)h≤ε.\frac{L_{\Pi}(h;I)}{h}\leq\varepsilon.

Intuitively, gg specifies the required convergence speed: g⁡(t∗)g(t_{*}) controls the length of the post-event window needed to make the expected fraction of mismatched rounds small. For each ε\varepsilon, the same coefficient cεc_{\varepsilon} must work for every legal instance. The condition still allows mismatches caused by later maintenance.

Corollary 1 (Recovery of flexible SC-DA).

For every K≥2K\geq 2 and every nondecreasing, polynomial-time computable g:ℕ≥1→ℕ≥1g:\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}\to\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1} with g⁡(t)=Ω⁡(t)g(t)=\Omega(t), the protocol Πg\Pi_{g} in Theorem 2 has sublinear mismatch cost relative to gg.

This follows by bounding recovery and subsequent maintenance within each post-event window; the proof is in Appendix A.7. In particular, the original SC-DA satisfies the condition for the linear function g⁡(t)=tg(t)=t.

The lower bound requires only that gg be a nondecreasing positive integer function. For such functions, use the same recurrence (6) to define Ng​(T)N_{g}(T).

Theorem 3 (Necessary mismatch cost).

For every K≥2K\geq 2, every nondecreasing g:ℕ≥1→ℕ≥1g:\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}\to\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}, and every legal randomized adaptive protocol Π\Pi with sublinear mismatch cost relative to gg, the following bounds hold.

There is a two-player static instance I0I_{0}, such that

𝔼​DΠ​(T,I0)=Ω⁡(Ng​(T))(T→∞).\mathbb{E}D_{\Pi}(T;I_{0})=\Omega(N_{g}(T))\qquad(T\to\infty).

For every t∗≥2t_{*}\geq 2, there exists a dynamic instance I′I^{\prime} with last population-event time t∗t_{*} such that, for every T≥t∗T\geq t_{*},

𝔼​DΠ​(T,I′)=Ω⁡(t∗+Ng​(T)).\mathbb{E}D_{\Pi}(T;I^{\prime})=\Omega\!\left(t_{*}+N_{g}(T)\right). (9)
Proof idea.

We use a two-player market where detecting a hidden departure requires trying the other player’s arm, causing a mismatch if nobody leaves. The recovery requirement limits how long these tests can be postponed, yielding the static bound. For the dynamic bound, population changes first force transient mismatches, after which the same argument forces maintenance costs in the final fixed market. Both costs therefore arise on the same instance. The full proof appears in Section B.1.

For every fixed function gg covered by Theorem 2, the constructed protocol Πg\Pi_{g} achieves worst-case static mismatch Θ​(Ng​(T))\Theta(N_{g}(T)) as T→∞T\to\infty. Theorem 3 gives a matching Ω​(Ng​(T))\Omega(N_{g}(T)) lower bound for every fixed protocol satisfying Definition 1.

For the linear function g⁡(t)=tg(t)=t, the dynamic lower bound in Theorem 3 matches the dependence on t∗t_{*} and TT achieved by SC-DA in Theorem 1, for fixed KK, t∗≥2t_{*}\geq 2, and T≥t∗T\geq t_{*}.

5 Dynamic Matching with Two-Sided Learning

5.1 Setting and Guarantee

We now consider the two-sided learning setting, where both players and arms initially lack knowledge of their own true utilities and preference rankings. We introduce Self-Calibrating Preference Certification (SC-PC), which combines local coordination with learning from accepted interactions to maintain the POSM under population changes. We use the model of Section 2.2, with fixed strict preferences induced by the utility means and a population path independent of rewards and protocol randomness. Accepted rewards lie in [0,1][0,1] with fixed means conditional on the past and current proposals and acceptance decisions; rejections give no samples.

Each agent runs SC-PC using only KK, its own local clock, and its local observations. Arms retain their own private handles and statistics and follow the stateful service in Section C.1, which may accept lower-utility requesters for sampling. Section 5.2 explains the protocol’s design and local behavior; Appendix C.2 gives the complete local algorithms. For a nonempty final population 𝒫∞\mathcal{P}_{\infty}, let m∗m^{*} be its POSM and set Ei∗={x∈𝒦:μi,x≥μi,m∗​(i)}E_{i}^{*}=\{x\in\mathcal{K}:\mu_{i,x}\geq\mu_{i,m^{*}(i)}\}. The minimum relevant gap is

Δmin=min⁡(CLOSE\displaystyle\Delta_{\min}=\min\Bigl( {1}∪{μi,x−μi,z:i∈𝒫∞,x∈Ei∗,z∈𝒦,μi,x>μi,z}\displaystyle\{1\}\cup\{\mu_{i,x}-\mu_{i,z}:i\in\mathcal{P}_{\infty},\ x\in E_{i}^{*},\ z\in\mathcal{K},\ \mu_{i,x}>\mu_{i,z}\} (11)
∪{|πx,i−πx,j|:i,j∈𝒫∞,i≠j,x∈Ei∗∩Ej∗}).\displaystyle}{\displaystyle\cup\{|\pi_{x,i}-\pi_{x,j}|:i,j\in\mathcal{P}_{\infty},\ i\neq j,\ x\in E_{i}^{*}\cap E_{j}^{*}\}\Bigr).

Empty comparison families are omitted. Strict preferences give Δmin>0\Delta_{\min}>0. Using the minimum over all final-market comparisons gives a weaker bound.

Theorem 4 (Two-sided learning and dynamic POSM matching).

Under this setting, fix K≥2K\geq 2 and any legal finite-event instance II with at most KK active players per round and last population-event time t∗t_{*}. For every integer T≥1T\geq 1, if the final population is nonempty, SC-PC satisfies

𝔼​D​(T,I)=O⁡(t∗+K4​Δmin−2​log⁡T).\mathbb{E}D(T;I)=O\!\left(t_{*}+K^{4}\Delta_{\min}^{-2}\log T\right).

The bound holds with the same constant for all admissible parameters, instances, and reward processes. Neither TT, t∗t_{*}, nor Δmin\Delta_{\min} is an input. If the final population is empty, then D⁡(T,I)≤min⁡{T,t∗}D(T;I)\leq\min\{T,t_{*}\}.

The complete proof of Theorem 4 is given in Appendix C.7.

For the statistical lower bound, call a protocol uniformly efficient if its decision rules are fixed without the unknown means and it has 𝔼​D​(T,I)=o⁡(Tα)\mathbb{E}D(T;I)=o(T^{\alpha}) for every α>0\alpha>0 on every fixed static strict Bernoulli instance. In the following claim, log\log denotes the base-two logarithm.

Claim 1 (Static statistical lower bound).

Fix K≥2K\geq 2 and 0<Δ≤min⁡{1/8,1/[4​(K−1)]}0<\Delta\leq\min\{1/8,1/[4(K-1)]\}. There is a static KK-player instance II, depending only on K,ΔK,\Delta, with a unique stable matching and Δmin=Δ\Delta_{\min}=\Delta, such that every uniformly efficient protocol Π\Pi satisfies

lim infT→∞𝔼​DΠ​(T,I)log⁡T≥K−14​Δ2.\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{\mathbb{E}D_{\Pi}(T;I)}{\log T}\geq\frac{K-1}{4\Delta^{2}}.

By Theorem 4, SC-PC has O⁡(log⁡T)O(\log T) expected mismatch on every fixed static strict Bernoulli instance and is therefore uniformly efficient. Static instances are legal dynamic instances. Thus, for fixed KK, its upper bound matches the logarithmic horizon and inverse-square gap orders required on this family, with T→∞T\to\infty taken for each fixed Δ\Delta. No optimality in KK is claimed.

The construction and change-of-measure proof [KCG16], together with the comparison with binary-stability bounds [Bas25], appear in Appendix D.

5.2 Protocol Overview and Design Rationale

SC-PC retains SC-DA’s collection-work-replay structure. With unknown preferences, a rejection need not reveal a true preference comparison. Both endpoints therefore accumulate evidence from every acceptance across all modes. Confidence comparisons retain options not yet ruled out as best; under valid comparisons, a singleton certifies the best option in the current set.

Player modes.

Seek uses BUS feedback to enter Work or Root. Root clears earlier work and gathers replaying players for a new computation. During Work, players explore unresolved comparisons, hold certified arms, and remove arms only under the prescribed rejection rule. Replay repeats the final actual work proposal. Every output updates a persistent replay scale from local output intervals. The next replay uses this scale if the final request to a held arm is accepted, and a minimum grace otherwise. Rejection may shorten the deadline subject to that grace, and expiry returns the player to Seek.

Arm service and safe deletion.

Every arm, including BUS and PARK, uses Control service to support coordination through a fixed private priority order, and Business service to sample among confidence candidates. In either state, it accepts the eligible requester whose last acceptance is oldest; transitions depend only on requests and its local clock. During coordinated work in a fixed market with valid comparisons, this service and the spacing of exploratory requests ensure that each permitted deletion has a witness: another holder whom the arm prefers to the deleting player. Thus no stable-matching edge is deleted, and distinct held arms for all players yield the POSM. Appendix C.1 gives the precise rules and Appendix C.2 their pseudocode.

Learning progress and cost.

Along a consecutive episode chain in the final market satisfying the coordination and confidence conditions in Appendices C.3 and C.4.1, failed episodes add permanent samples, limiting their number to O⁡(Δmin−2​log⁡T)O(\Delta_{\min}^{-2}\log T), while replay-scale growth limits successful ones to O⁡(log⁡T)O(\log T). Each interval between coordinated replays costs O⁡(K4)O(K^{4}) mismatches. Concentration and recovery from histories affected by statistical errors control the remaining expected cost, yielding Theorem 4.

Appendix A Analysis of SC-DA

This appendix proves Lemmas 1, 2 and 3 and Corollary 1. We first establish matching correctness and calibration for mature executions, then prove recovery and bounded maintenance under a general replay rule. We finally verify the properties of the rule FgF_{g} defined in (5) and prove its post-event guarantee.

Fix K≥2K\geq 2, with J=K2+5​K+1J=K^{2}+5K+1 and H=4​J+4H=4J+4 as in Algorithm 1. For the analysis, allow any nondecreasing computable replay rule F:ℕ≥1→ℕ≥1F:\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}\to\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1} satisfying

F⁡(x)≥H+2​x(x≥1).F(x)\geq H+2x\qquad(x\geq 1). (12)

Keep all control rules unchanged. At every actual output, with final proposed arm yy, replace only the replay-length update by

L←F⁡(a−ℓ),q←a+L,ℓ←a.L\leftarrow F(a-\ell),\qquad q\leftarrow a+L,\qquad\ell\leftarrow a. (13)

The update uses the old ℓ\ell, even if the output is incorrect or the final proposal is rejected. The original SC-DA uses F⁡(x)=H+2​xF(x)=H+2x. The protocol Πg\Pi_{g} uses F=FgF=F_{g}; the required properties of FgF_{g} are verified in Appendix A.6.

A.1 Local Protocol Rules

We use Algorithm 1 with the replay update in (13) and record the local conventions used below. A player’s persistent state consists of its preference ranking, local age aa, saved arm yy, previous output age ℓ\ell, and BUS-acceptance counter ρ\rho. At birth,

a=ℓ=ρ=0,m=Seek.a=\ell=\rho=0,\qquad m=\textnormal{{Seek}}. (14)

The pending mode ν\nu and rejection flag 𝑠𝑒𝑒𝑛𝑅\mathit{seenR} are initially 𝗇𝗈𝗇𝖾\mathsf{none} and 𝖿𝖺𝗅𝗌𝖾\mathsf{false}, respectively; mode-specific registers are initialized on entry.

Round order and mode entry.

Population events occur first and are not announced to players. Before proposing, each player applies its pending mode change and clears ν\nu, checks expiration of its Replay deadline qq, and checks sweep qualification, in that order. Expiration at a≥qa\geq q returns the player to Seek; qualification applies only in Seek with ρ=J\rho=J. Thus expiration can lead to Sweep in the same round, while qualification never interrupts Work. The player then makes one proposal, updates ρ\rho, processes feedback in its current mode, and increments aa. Feedback-triggered mode changes take effect next round. Round-start states below are taken after these checks and before proposals.

Mode entry preserves a,y,ℓ,ρa,y,\ell,\rho. A fresh Seek visit clears 𝑠𝑒𝑒𝑛𝑅\mathit{seenR}; Sweep starts with s=1s=1 and 𝑏𝑙𝑜𝑐𝑘𝑂𝐾=𝗍𝗋𝗎𝖾\mathit{blockOK}=\mathsf{true}; Work starts with h=0,k=1h=0,k=1; and Replay retains the deadline computed at output. Only an actual output changes ℓ\ell.

BUS feedback and replay.

In every mode, an accepted BUS proposal sets ρ←min⁡{J,ρ+1}\rho\leftarrow\min\{J,\rho+1\}; every other proposal resets ρ\rho to zero, even after saturation. In Seek, the player proposes to BUS: a rejection sets 𝑠𝑒𝑒𝑛𝑅=𝗍𝗋𝗎𝖾\mathit{seenR}=\mathsf{true}, and an acceptance with this flag set and updated ρ≥2\rho\geq 2 schedules Work through an AA handoff. In Replay, the player proposes to yy; acceptance leaves the deadline unchanged, while rejection schedules Seek.

Sweep blocks.

Each block follows the 2​K2K-entry scan word (3). A BUS rejection schedules Seek and skips every block-completion test, including at s=2​Ks=2K. A non-BUS rejection marks the block as failed but does not interrupt it. At completion, an all-accepted block schedules Work; otherwise, a new block starts next round. Thus a continuing sweep leaves BUS only for isolated one-round gaps, including across failed-block restarts.

Work and output.

A Work invocation lasts exactly JJ rounds, indexed by h=0,…,J−1h=0,\ldots,J-1. It proposes to PARK in Park for h<2​Kh<2K, to pi​(1)p_{i}(1) in Top for 2​K≤h≤4​K2K\leq h\leq 4K, and to pi​(k)p_{i}(k) in DA for 4​K<h<J4K<h<J. Only a rejection in a nonfinal DA round advances kk, capped at KK. The final round saves the actual proposed arm and performs (13), then schedules Replay. The argument of FF is always positive: the first output has ℓ=0\ell=0 and a≥J−1>0a\geq J-1>0, and later outputs occur at strictly greater local ages than the output recorded in ℓ\ell.

A.2 Correctness and Calibration of Mature Executions

For this subsection, fix a nonempty market of n≤Kn\leq K players, labeled 1,…,n1,\ldots,n in decreasing priority at BUS. Player 11 is the root, and m∗m^{*} is the market’s POSM. These labels and global round numbers are only for analysis; players need not know their BUS ranks or detect mature entry.

Definition 2 (Mature entry).

After the round-start updates in round cc and before proposals, suppose the root has just entered Work, while every other player is in Seek with ρ=0\rho=0 and a BUS rejection recorded during its current Seek visit. Then cc is a mature entry, and the computation it initiates is a mature execution.

With the staggered entry times below, the Top stages share a round in which every player proposes to its first-choice arm. The following lemma proves correctness of the ensuing DA updates, and Lemma 5 establishes the entry times and the replay handoff.

Lemma 4 (Deferred Acceptance with Delayed Proposals).

Suppose player jj starts Work at sj=c+2​(j−1)s_{j}=c+2(j-1), no population event occurs in [c,o1)[c,o_{1}), where o1=c+J−1o_{1}=c+J-1, and all players are in Top with application index 11 at t0=maxj⁡sj+2​Kt_{0}=\max_{j}s_{j}+2K. On [t0,o1)[t_{0},o_{1}), the execution implements player-proposing deferred acceptance with delayed proposals. Every rejection processed in DA excludes its edge from every stable matching. An arm that rejects a player retains an acceptor preferred to that player through round o1−1o_{1}-1. An all-accepted round occurs by c+J−2c+J-2; its matching is m∗m^{*} and persists through round o1−1o_{1}-1.

Proof.

Call a rejection adopted when it is processed in a nonfinal DA round. On consecutive rounds of [t0,o1)[t_{0},o_{1}), every accepted player repeats its arm, including across the Top–DA transition. If displaced, it is replaced by a proposer the arm prefers. Thus an arm’s acceptor can only improve after its first acceptance in this interval.

For rejection validity, induct on rounds from t0t_{0}, when all application indices are 11. Suppose ii adopts a rejection by arm xx, whose winner is ww. Every arm that ww prefers to xx was passed after an adopted rejection in a strictly earlier round; this set is empty if ww is still in Top. By induction, none can be ww’s partner in a stable matching mm. If m⁡(i)=xm(i)=x, then ww prefers xx to m⁡(w)m(w), and xx prefers ww to ii, so (w,x)(w,x) blocks mm. This contradiction uses only rejections from earlier rounds.

A rejection at a player’s last arm would require better actual acceptors at all KK arms, by persistence at its previously rejected arms. These would be KK distinct other players, contradicting n≤Kn\leq K. Hence the cap never prevents an advance, and at most n⁡(K−1)n(K-1) advances occur. Rejected proposals are repeated during Top; otherwise these are player-proposing DA updates.

All players are in DA by t1=c+6​K−1t_{1}=c+6K-1, and

t1+n⁡(K−1)≤c+6​K−1+K⁡(K−1)=c+J−2<o1.t_{1}+n(K-1)\leq c+6K-1+K(K-1)=c+J-2<o_{1}. (15)

Every round in [t1,t1+n⁡(K−1)][t_{1},t_{1}+n(K-1)] without universal acceptance produces an advance. These n⁡(K−1)+1n(K-1)+1 rounds therefore include an all-accepted round.

Let MM be the matching in an all-accepted round. Every arm that a player prefers to its partner has rejected that player and retains a better acceptor, so MM is stable. Rejection validity also excludes every such preferred edge from all stable matchings, proving M=m∗M=m^{*}. Repeated accepted proposals preserve this matching through round o1−1o_{1}-1. ∎

Lemma 5 (Correctness and Output Offsets of Mature Executions).

Suppose cc is a mature entry and no population event occurs from cc through V=c+J+2​(n−1)V=c+J+2(n-1). Player jj starts Work and outputs at

sj=c+2​(j−1),oj=c+J−1+2​(j−1)=o1+2​(j−1).s_{j}=c+2(j-1),\qquad o_{j}=c+J-1+2(j-1)=o_{1}+2(j-1).

Proof.

Entry and output times. At mature entry, each remaining seeker has a recorded BUS rejection and ρ=0\rho=0. While earlier entrants stay in Park, the highest-priority remaining seeker receives two consecutive BUS acceptances and enters Work next round. Induction gives

sj=c+2​(j−1),1≤j≤n.s_{j}=c+2(j-1),\qquad 1\leq j\leq n. (16)

For n≥2n\geq 2, the last qualifying pair ends at c+2​n−3≤c+2​K−3c+2n-3\leq c+2K-3, before the root leaves Park at c+2​Kc+2K. Each seeker takes its AA handoff before accumulating the J>2J>2 acceptances needed for a sweep. The case n=1n=1 is immediate.

oj=sj+J−1=o1+2​(j−1),o1=c+J−1.o_{j}=s_{j}+J-1=o_{1}+2(j-1),\qquad o_{1}=c+J-1. (17)

Output and replay. Every output assigns a replay length at least HH, so each new global deadline is at least oj+H≥o1+Ho_{j}+H\geq o_{1}+H. Since

V=on+1=o1+2​(n−1)+1≤o1+2​K−1<o1+H,V=o_{n}+1=o_{1}+2(n-1)+1\leq o_{1}+2K-1<o_{1}+H,

no replay expires during the replay handoff. Inductively, players still in Work repeat their accepted arms and save them at output, while players already in Replay propose to those same arms and remain accepted. Hence the matching stays at m∗m^{*} through VV. Each player outputs exactly once, enters Replay at oj+1o_{j}+1, and remains there through VV. ∎

Calibration from consecutive outputs.

Consider any two mature executions in this fixed market that give consecutive actual outputs for every player. Let om−1,omo_{m-1},o_{m} be the root’s output rounds in these executions. By Lemma 5, player jj, born at bjb_{j}, outputs at local ages aj,s=os+2​(j−1)−bja_{j,s}=o_{s}+2(j-1)-b_{j} for s∈{m−1,m}s\in\{m-1,m\}. aj,m−ℓj=om−om−1,Lm=F⁡(om−om−1).a_{j,m}-\ell_{j}=o_{m}-o_{m-1},\qquad L_{m}=F(o_{m}-o_{m-1}).

Thus the replay lengths agree, while the global deadlines retain the output offsets:

Qj,m=om+2​(j−1)+Lm.Q_{j,m}=o_{m}+2(j-1)+L_{m}. (18)

A replay handoff with a common replay length is called calibrated.

A.3 Sweep Isolation and Mature Entry

The next lemma shows that a sweep accepted at every BUS proposal isolates the other players, and that a successful block followed by an event-free round establishes a mature entry. Its isolation property will also bound recovery time.

Lemma 6 (Sweep isolation and mature entry).

Consider a history of Algorithm 1 with the update (13), reachable from the prescribed initialization, and let player zz enter Sweep in global round bb.

  1. (i)

    Isolation during a continuing sweep. Suppose zz remains in this visit through round dd and is accepted at every BUS action in rounds b,…,db,\ldots,d. At the start of bb, after all round-start checks, every other present player is in Seek or Replay, with ρ=0\rho=0 and no pending Work entry. Throughout b,…,db,\ldots,d, all other players remain in Seek or Replay and never schedule Work; in particular, none enters Sweep or produces an output. Population events and failed blocks are allowed.

  2. (ii)

    Mature entry after success. If this visit completes an all-accepted block in round ee, and no population event occurs in round c=e+1c=e+1, then cc is a mature entry with zz as root. Population events during qualification and the sweep, including at the start of round ee, are allowed.

Proof.

Proof of (i). Put v=b−Jv=b-J. Since every action other than an accepted BUS proposal resets ρ\rho, even after saturation, qualification at bb implies that zz is accepted at BUS in

v,v+1,…,b−1.v,v+1,\ldots,b-1. (19)

No other player can complete an AA pair or a successful block in this interval, since both require a final BUS acceptance. Thus no other Work entry is scheduled.

Any Work entry pending from v−1v-1 takes effect at vv, so all earlier Work invocations finish by v+J−1=b−1v+J-1=b-1. A competing sweep present at vv reaches BUS by v+1v+1 and, if still present, returns to Seek by v+2v+2. Every other player’s counter is reset in each qualification round, excluding new sweeps in v+1,…,bv+1,\ldots,b. Since J>2J>2, all other players are in Seek or Replay at bb, with zero counters and no pending Work. Arrivals start in Seek with ρ=0\rho=0, and departures simply remove players.

The scan word (3) leaves BUS only for isolated single rounds, including across failed-block restarts. Non-BUS rejections mark a block as failed without restarting it. Since zz wins every BUS action, every other player’s consecutive BUS-acceptance count stays at most one. Thus neither an AA handoff nor a new sweep qualification is possible, and all other players remain in Seek or Replay. This proves (i) on every continuing prefix, regardless of eventual success.

Proof of (ii). On a BUS rejection, the player skips the block-completion test and leaves Sweep in the following round. Thus a visit completing a successful block at ee has only BUS acceptances, and (i) applies with d=ed=e. No other output occurs: each old replay keeps its saved arm until it ends, and no seeker reenters Replay. A player still replaying when its saved arm is visited is rejected. Every arm is visited by e−2e-2, so all old replays have ended by e−1e-1; later arrivals start in Seek.

The final two proposals are to BUS. In round ee, every other present player, including any new arrival, therefore proposes to BUS and is rejected. Each ends the round in Seek with a rejection recorded during its current visit, ρ=0\rho=0, and no pending Work. Since zz wins against all these players, it is the highest-ranked player at BUS. With no population event at c=e+1c=e+1, its scheduled Work entry establishes the mature entry in Definition 2. ∎

A.4 Proof of Lemma 1

To apply the calibration identity, we must obtain two mature executions whose outputs are consecutive for every player in the final market. For the replay rule FF satisfying (12), define the nondecreasing recovery map

ΨF​(x)=x+F⁡(x+H)+3​H.\Psi_{F}(x)=x+F(x+H)+3H. (20)

Replay expires in its deadline round; acceptance never extends it, and rejection can end it earlier.

A fresh Seek visit clears that record and cannot trigger an AA handoff. By (22), every preceding replay ends by t∗+J+2+F⁡(t∗+J+2)t_{*}+J+2+F(t_{*}+J+2). β≤t∗+J+2+F⁡(t∗+J+2)+J≤ΨF​(t∗+1).\beta\leq t_{*}+J+2+F(t_{*}+J+2)+J\leq\Psi_{F}(t_{*}+1). (23)

If no entry has occurred by that round, all current replays have ended. A winning seeker continues on BUS, including upon sweep qualification; a player accepted while replaying BUS proposes there again, including after expiration; and a continuing sweep leaves BUS only for isolated rounds. A Work entry in either intervening round would contradict the choice of rr. This two-round absence is impossible, so the first new Work entry follows a successful sweep and is mature by Lemma 6(ii).

≤Vfirst+F⁡(Vfirst)+2​J+6​K−2\displaystyle\leq V_{\mathrm{first}}+F(V_{\mathrm{first}})+2J+6K-2

After calibration, each maintenance window starts at the root’s replay deadline and ends at the next replay handoff. We show that these windows have bounded length and preserve calibration.

Appendix B Lower Bounds and Optimality

This appendix proves Theorem 3 and the iteration-count results in Section 4.2, and gives the computational details for the exponential function. We use the known-preference setting, in which each arm accepts its most-preferred proposer in each round. The lower bounds allow private state, private randomness, adaptive proposals, and accepted utilities.

B.1 Proof of Theorem 3

Proof of Theorem 3.

Fix K,g,ΠK,g,\Pi as in the theorem.

Static bound.

In the static instance I0I_{0}, players p1,p2p_{1},p_{2} enter in round 11 and remain forever, both ranking 0≻1≻⋯≻K−10\succ 1\succ\cdots\succ K-1. Arm 00 prefers p1p_{1} to p2p_{2}; every other arm prefers p2p_{2} to p1p_{1}. Acceptance on arm xx gives either player deterministic utility (K−x)/(K+1)(K-x)/(K+1). The unique stable matching is {(p1,0),(p2,1)}\{(p_{1},0),(p_{2},1)\}. For each τ≥2\tau\geq 2, let IτI_{\tau} remove p1p_{1} at the start of round τ\tau; thereafter the POSM assigns p2p_{2} to 00. This family is fixed independently of the protocol, function gg, recovery coefficient, and horizon.

Write

m⁡(T)=𝔼​DΠ​(T,I0),LΠ​(h,Iτ)=𝔼⁡[DΠ​(τ+h,Iτ)−DΠ​(τ,Iτ)].m(T)=\mathbb{E}D_{\Pi}(T;I_{0}),\qquad L_{\Pi}(h;I_{\tau})=\mathbb{E}[D_{\Pi}(\tau+h;I_{\tau})-D_{\Pi}(\tau;I_{\tau})].

Couple the executions using identical private random tapes. The two histories agree before τ\tau. Until p2p_{2}’s first proposal to 00 at or after τ\tau, every other arm accepts it in both executions with identical utility, independently of p1p_{1}’s actions. Induction preserves its local state, clock, and random-tape consumption through the selection of that first proposal, before its feedback is observed. The proposal is therefore made in the same round in both executions; its feedback may differ, and no subsequent agreement is needed.

In the static execution, every proposal by p2p_{2} to 00 causes mismatch. The expected number of such proposals in {τ,…,τ+h}\{\tau,\ldots,\tau+h\} is at most m⁡(τ+h)−m⁡(τ−1)m(\tau+h)-m(\tau-1). With probability at least max⁡{0,1−m⁡(τ+h)+m⁡(τ−1)}\max\{0,1-m(\tau+h)+m(\tau-1)\}, there is no such proposal. On that event all hh rounds τ+1,…,τ+h\tau+1,\ldots,\tau+h are mismatched in the departure execution. Therefore

LΠ​(h,Iτ)≥h​max⁡{0,1−m⁡(τ+h)+m⁡(τ−1)},τ≥2,h≥1.L_{\Pi}(h;I_{\tau})\geq h\max\{0,1-m(\tau+h)+m(\tau-1)\},\qquad\tau\geq 2,\ h\geq 1. (37)

Including τ\tau in the static charge accounts for detection in the event round, which the recovery cost itself excludes.

In particular, (37) implies

LΠ​(h,Iτ)≤h/2⟹m⁡(τ+h)−m⁡(τ−1)≥1/2.L_{\Pi}(h;I_{\tau})\leq h/2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad m(\tau+h)-m(\tau-1)\geq 1/2. (38)

Choose a half-accuracy coefficient c1/2>0c_{1/2}>0 supplied by Definition 1, and put q=max⁡{1,⌈c1/2⌉}q=\max\{1,\lceil c_{1/2}\rceil\}. Define

x0=2,hj=q​g​(xj),xj+1=xj+hj+1.x_{0}=2,\qquad h_{j}=qg(x_{j}),\qquad x_{j+1}=x_{j}+h_{j}+1.

The recovery window of IxjI_{x_{j}} is {xj+1,…,xj+1−1}\{x_{j}+1,\ldots,x_{j+1}-1\}, of length hjh_{j}. Since hj≥c1/2​g​(xj)h_{j}\geq c_{1/2}g(x_{j}), the recovery condition bounds its expected cost by hj/2h_{j}/2. Equation (38) therefore forces at least 1/21/2 expected static mismatch in the augmented interval {xj,…,xj+1−1}\{x_{j},\ldots,x_{j+1}-1\}. These intervals are disjoint. If

n⁡(T)=#⁡{j:xj+1≤T+1},n(T)=\#\{j:x_{j+1}\leq T+1\},

then m⁡(T)≥n⁡(T)/2m(T)\geq n(T)/2, since all these intervals lie among the first TT rounds.

Let Φ⁡(x)=x+g⁡(x)\Phi(x)=x+g(x), and recall r0=2r_{0}=2. Since gg is nondecreasing and positive,

Φ∘(q+1)​(x)≥x+(q+1)​g​(x)≥x+q​g​(x)+1.\Phi^{\circ(q+1)}(x)\geq x+(q+1)g(x)\geq x+qg(x)+1.

Thus xj≤r(q+1)​jx_{j}\leq r_{(q+1)j}. Since xn⁡(T)+1>T+1x_{n(T)+1}>T+1, also r(q+1)​(n​(T)+1)>Tr_{(q+1)(n(T)+1)}>T, giving Ng​(T)≤(q+1)​(n⁡(T)+1)N_{g}(T)\leq(q+1)(n(T)+1). We have proved the uniform finite bound

𝔼​DΠ​(T,I0)≥12​max⁡{0,Ng​(T)q+1−1}(T≥0).\mathbb{E}D_{\Pi}(T;I_{0})\geq\frac{1}{2}\max\left\{0,\frac{N_{g}(T)}{q+1}-1\right\}\qquad(T\geq 0). (39)

Every iterate is finite, and the sequence is unbounded, so Ng​(T)→∞N_{g}(T)\to\infty. For fixed KK, the coefficient qq depends only on the chosen protocol and function gg. Thus (39) proves the static bound on the same instance I0I_{0} for every protocol.

Dynamic bound.

Fix t∗≥2t_{*}\geq 2. A permanent player bb enters in round 11. There is a potential fresh guard crc_{r} for each r=1,…,t∗r=1,\ldots,t_{*}. All players rank 0≻1≻⋯≻K−10\succ 1\succ\cdots\succ K-1. Arm 00 ranks every guard above bb, while every other arm ranks bb above every guard. Complete the orders among guards arbitrarily and fix consistent deterministic utilities. When bb is alone, its POSM assignment is 00; with a guard present, the unique stable matching assigns the guard to 00 and bb to 11.

Before execution, choose independent fair bits ξ1,…,ξt∗−1\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{t_{*}-1}, independently of the protocol’s private randomness. Guard crc_{r}, for r<t∗r<t_{*}, enters in round rr and leaves at the start of round r+1r+1 if ξr=1\xi_{r}=1, and never enters otherwise. In round t∗t_{*}, the fresh guard ct∗c_{t_{*}} enters and remains forever. At most two players are active in any round, each identity has one contiguous lifetime, and the last event is exactly at t∗t_{*}. Every player is initialized normally; the permanent player keeps its actual state throughout.

Before its round-rr proposal, for r<t∗r<t_{*}, player bb has no observation of ξr\xi_{r}. Conditional on the past, let p0,p1p_{0},p_{1} be its probabilities of proposing to arms 0,10,1. Correct matching requires proposal 00 when ξr=0\xi_{r}=0, and proposal 11 when ξr=1\xi_{r}=1. Its conditional probability of making the required proposal is at most

12​p0+12​p1≤12,\tfrac{1}{2}p_{0}+\tfrac{1}{2}p_{1}\leq\tfrac{1}{2},

regardless of the guard’s actions. Averaging over the preselected bit strings therefore gives one fixed instance I′I^{\prime} such that, writing m⁡(T)=𝔼​DΠ​(T,I′)m(T)=\mathbb{E}D_{\Pi}(T;I^{\prime}),

m⁡(T)≥m⁡(t∗−1)≥t∗−12≥t∗4(T≥t∗).m(T)\geq m(t_{*}-1)\geq\frac{t_{*}-1}{2}\geq\frac{t_{*}}{4}\qquad(T\geq t_{*}). (40)

This choice depends on the protocol’s distribution and t∗t_{*}, but not on its realized random tape or on TT.

For each τ≥t∗+1\tau\geq t_{*}+1, form a comparison instance Iτ′I^{\prime}_{\tau} by keeping the entire history of I′I^{\prime} before τ\tau and removing ct∗c_{t_{*}} at the start of round τ\tau. Its last event is τ\tau. Couple the two executions with identical private random tapes. Until bb’s first proposal to 00 at or after τ\tau, every other arm accepts it in both executions with the same utility, so its local history and state agree. Such a proposal causes mismatch in I′I^{\prime}; without it, every post-departure round is mismatched in Iτ′I^{\prime}_{\tau}. The same event-round accounting as in (37) gives

LΠ​(h,Iτ′)≥h​max⁡{0,1−m⁡(τ+h)+m⁡(τ−1)}(τ≥t∗+1,h≥1).L_{\Pi}(h;I^{\prime}_{\tau})\geq h\max\{0,1-m(\tau+h)+m(\tau-1)\}\qquad(\tau\geq t_{*}+1,\ h\geq 1). (41)

This coupling preserves the actual states inherited at t∗t_{*}.

With the same coefficient qq, let

j⋆=min⁡{j:rj≥t∗+1},x0=rj⋆,xj+1=xj+q​g​(xj)+1.j_{\star}=\min\{j:r_{j}\geq t_{*}+1\},\qquad x_{0}=r_{j_{\star}},\qquad x_{j+1}=x_{j}+qg(x_{j})+1.

Since rj≥j+2r_{j}\geq j+2, we have j⋆≤t∗−1j_{\star}\leq t_{*}-1. Apply the recovery condition to Ixj′I^{\prime}_{x_{j}} with window length q​g​(xj)qg(x_{j}). Equation (41) forces at least 1/21/2 expected mismatch in each augmented interval {xj,…,xj+1−1}\{x_{j},\ldots,x_{j+1}-1\}. These intervals are disjoint and start after the population prefix. If

n⁡(T)=#⁡{j:xj+1≤T+1},n(T)=\#\{j:x_{j+1}\leq T+1\},

then n⁡(T)≤2​m​(T)n(T)\leq 2m(T). The iteration comparison used for the static bound yields

xj≤rj⋆+(q+1)​j,Ng​(T)≤j⋆+(q+1)​(n⁡(T)+1).x_{j}\leq r_{j_{\star}+(q+1)j},\qquad N_{g}(T)\leq j_{\star}+(q+1)(n(T)+1).

The latter inequality also holds when no augmented interval is complete. By (40), t∗≤4​m​(T)t_{*}\leq 4m(T) and 1≤2​m​(T)1\leq 2m(T). Consequently,

Ng​(T)≤4​m​(T)+4​(q+1)​m​(T)≤8​(q+1)​m​(T).N_{g}(T)\leq 4m(T)+4(q+1)m(T)\leq 8(q+1)m(T).

𝔼​DΠ​(T,I′)≥t∗+Ng​(T)12​(q+1)(T≥t∗≥2).\mathbb{E}D_{\Pi}(T;I^{\prime})\geq\frac{t_{*}+N_{g}(T)}{12(q+1)}\qquad(T\geq t_{*}\geq 2). (42)

The coefficient is independent of t∗t_{*} and TT, and the selected instance works for all T≥t∗T\geq t_{*}, proving the dynamic bound. ∎

The static bound also rules out sublinear mismatch cost relative to a bounded function gg. Indeed, suppose K≥2K\geq 2 and g⁡(t)≤Gg(t)\leq G for all tt, for some fixed positive integer GG. Then rj≤2+j​Gr_{j}\leq 2+jG, so Ng​(T)=Ω​(T)N_{g}(T)=\Omega(T). If Π\Pi satisfied Definition 1, (39) would give m⁡(T)=𝔼​DΠ​(T,I0)=Ω⁡(T)m(T)=\mathbb{E}D_{\Pi}(T;I_{0})=\Omega(T). On the same static instance, t∗=1t_{*}=1, and the recovery condition gives m⁡(1+h)−m⁡(1)≤ε​hm(1+h)-m(1)\leq\varepsilon h for every ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1) and h≥cε​g​(1)h\geq c_{\varepsilon}g(1). Hence m⁡(T)=o⁡(T)m(T)=o(T), a contradiction.

At g⁡(t)=tg(t)=t, the iteration is rj=2j+1r_{j}=2^{j+1}, and t∗+Ng​(T)=Θ⁡(t∗+log⁡T)t_{*}+N_{g}(T)=\Theta(t_{*}+\log T) uniformly for T≥t∗≥2T\geq t_{*}\geq 2. Together with Theorems 1 and 1, this proves the stated per-protocol optimality for fixed KK. The lower constant can depend on the fixed protocol’s recovery coefficient; a uniform comparison requires a common coefficient.

Positivity implies that g⁡(t)≥δg​tg(t)\geq\delta_{g}t for every t≥1t\geq 1, for some constant δg>0\delta_{g}>0. Ng~​(T)≤Ng​(T)≤d​Ng~​(T)(T≥0).N_{\widetilde{g}}(T)\leq N_{g}(T)\leq dN_{\widetilde{g}}(T)\qquad(T\geq 0).

Qg​(x)=x+g⁡(x),d=max⁡{1,⌈c⌉}.Q_{g}(x)=x+g(x),\qquad d=\max\{1,\lceil c\rceil\}.

Qg​(x)≤Qg~​(x)≤Qg∘d​(x).Q_{g}(x)\leq Q_{\widetilde{g}}(x)\leq Q_{g}^{\circ d}(x).

Iterating from 22 gives the claimed inequalities. B.3 The Exponential Function

Iteration count.

For g⁡(t)=2tg(t)=2^{t}, let E⁡(x)=2xE(x)=2^{x}. Since E⁡(x)≤x+2x≤E∘2​(x)E(x)\leq x+2^{x}\leq E^{\circ 2}(x) for x≥2x\geq 2, monotone iteration gives E∘j​(2)≤rj≤E∘(2​j)​(2)E^{\circ j}(2)\leq r_{j}\leq E^{\circ(2j)}(2). With log∗⁡T=min⁡{m∈ℤ≥0:log∘m⁡T≤1}\log^{*}T=\min\{m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}:\log^{\circ m}T\leq 1\}, the horizon sandwich gives (log∗⁡T−1)/2≤Ng​(T)≤log∗⁡T(\log^{*}T-1)/2\leq N_{g}(T)\leq\log^{*}T for T>2T>2. Hence Ng​(T)=Θ⁡(log∗⁡T)N_{g}(T)=\Theta(\log^{*}T).

Computation in local time.

The binary representation of 2t2^{t} has t+1t+1 bits, so g⁡(t)=2tg(t)=2^{t} is not polynomial-time computable from binary tt. From the unary input 1t1^{t}, it is computed in linear time by writing a one followed by tt zeros.

Fix KK and substitute this function into (5). To evaluate Fg​(x)F_{g}(x), generate the iterates starting at s0=Hs_{0}=H, evaluating 2sj2^{s_{j}} only while 64​sj≤x64s_{j}\leq x. Each such value has at most ⌊x/64⌋+1\lfloor x/64\rfloor+1 bits; the next iterate sj+2sjs_{j}+2^{s_{j}}, the candidate 2sj−sj2^{s_{j}}-s_{j}, and the running maximum all have O⁡(x)O(x) bits. Since sj+1≥2​sjs_{j+1}\geq 2s_{j}, at most O⁡(1+log⁡(x+1))O(1+\log(x+1)) eligible iterates are examined. If none is eligible, Fg​(x)=H+2​xF_{g}(x)=H+2x. Thus additions, comparisons, and writing the output take time polynomial in xx, with KK fixed. At each output, x=a−ℓ≤ax=a-\ell\leq a, so the new replay length and deadline have O⁡(a+1)O(a+1) bits and can be computed in time polynomial in the player’s local age. Between outputs, these stored values remain of polynomial bit length in the current age, so the remaining local updates also take polynomial time. This local-time bound does not satisfy the binary-input polynomial-time hypothesis of Theorem 2.

Appendix C The SC-PC Protocol and Its Analysis

We give the local implementation of SC-PC and prove Theorem 4. Sections C.1 and C.2 describe the protocol and the order of actions within a round.

A statistical error may delete a stable edge or lead to an incorrect replay. We therefore prove collection and recovery without assuming that earlier comparisons were correct. In a mature episode with covered comparisons, stable edges are preserved; failures add permanent samples, while successes force the replay scale to grow in subsequent episodes. These two forms of progress bound the cost along a chain of good episodes. Finally, concentration and two cold recoveries bound the expected time before such a chain begins.

All executions use the model of Section 2.2 and the prescribed initialization below; surviving players retain their actual states. The population path is fixed before rewards are generated, and each identity has one contiguous lifetime. Write 𝒫∞\mathcal{P}_{\infty} for the final population. Throughout this appendix, log\log is base two and ln\ln is the natural logarithm.

The last population-event time t∗t_{*} refers to the full schedule even when T≤t∗T\leq t_{*}. A static schedule has t∗=1t_{*}=1; a permanently empty market has zero cost. For integer endpoints 1≤s≤t1\leq s\leq t, write

D([s,t);I):=∑r=st−1𝟏{Mr≠mr∗}=D(t−1;I)−D(s−1;I).D([s,t);I):=\sum_{r=s}^{t-1}\mathbf{1}\{M_{r}\neq m_{r}^{*}\}=D(t-1;I)-D(s-1;I).

The protocol reads local age aa; physical round tt is used only in the analysis. Within work, hh counts completed rounds, so action h=0h=0 is the first work action. Permanent records and confidence decisions.

Each endpoint stores a count NxN_{x}, reward sum UxU_{x}, and last-acceptance time for each option: an arm for a player, or a permanent private player handle for an arm. Counts and sums start at zero and timestamps at −∞-\infty. Every acceptance, including a zero reward, updates both endpoints (Line 5 of Algorithm 3 and Lines 19–21 of Algorithm 4); rejection gives no sample. Records persist through mode changes and handle absence. Thus the two endpoints have the same edge count, denoted Ni​(x)N_{i}(x) for edge (i,x)(i,x).

At local age aa, define

θ^x={Ux/Nx,Nx>0,0,Nx=0,B⁡(a)=5​log⁡(a+2),βa​(x,z)=B⁡(a)2​(1Nx+1Nz).\widehat{\theta}_{x}=\begin{cases}U_{x}/N_{x},&N_{x}>0,\\ 0,&N_{x}=0,\end{cases}\qquad B(a)=5\log(a+2),\qquad\beta_{a}(x,z)=\sqrt{\frac{B(a)}{2}\left(\frac{1}{N_{x}}+\frac{1}{N_{z}}\right)}. (47)

Decisions use completed-round statistics. Every empirical maximizer belongs to Ca​(Q)C_{a}(Q), so it is nonempty. All comparisons matter: comparing only against one empirical maximizer need not give the same set.

Arm service.

Every arm, including BUS and PARK, follows Algorithm 3. Its clock starts at its first request and advances even in empty rounds; initially a=e=λ=0a=e=\lambda=0. For nonempty requester set RR, the eligible set is

Q={Ca​(R),λ>0,R,λ=0​ and ​a≡0(modGL),{min≺⁡R},λ=0​ and ​a≢0(modGL),Q=\begin{cases}C_{a}(R),&\lambda>0,\\ R,&\lambda=0\text{ and }a\equiv 0\pmod{G_{L}},\\ \{\min_{\prec}R\},&\lambda=0\text{ and }a\not\equiv 0\pmod{G_{L}},\end{cases} (49)

where ≺\prec is the arm’s private handle order. The arm accepts the eligible requester with the oldest acceptance timestamp, breaking ties by ≺\prec (Lines 3–4 of Algorithm 3). The counter ee records consecutive empty rounds; updated e≥2e\geq 2 refreshes the lease to τL\tau_{L} at round end, and otherwise the lease decreases toward zero (Lines 6–7 of the same algorithm). Thus business service starts after the second empty round, overrides fair control rounds, and is renewed by further empty rounds. Before startup the lease stays zero.

A new player sets a=0a=0, P=HLP=H_{L}, ℓ=⊥\ell=\bot, and enters fresh 𝖲𝖾𝖾𝗄\mathsf{Seek} (Lines 1–4 of Algorithm 4). The loop then applies scheduled transitions, checks replay expiry, makes one request, updates permanent records, and processes mode-specific feedback, in that order. Feedback transitions take effect next round; replay expiry changes the current request. Permanent records, PP, and ℓ\ell survive all transitions.

Collection.

The signed counter xx records consecutive BUS outcomes, ignoring non-BUS root requests. Fresh entry at age ww sets the following registers (Lines 1–5 of Algorithm 5):

x=0,𝖺𝗋𝗆𝖾𝖽=𝖿𝖺𝗅𝗌𝖾,b=w+EL,c=w+JL+χL+4.x=0,\qquad\mathsf{armed}=\mathsf{false},\qquad b=w+E_{L},\qquad c=w+J_{L}+\chi_{L}+4.

Qualification uses only ages a≥ba\geq b: KK consecutive post-guard rejections arm the player, and three consecutive post-guard acceptances send it to work if armed or to root otherwise. Guard feedback still updates xx and sets c=a+JL+χL+3c=a+J_{L}+\chi_{L}+3 whenever x≤−3x\leq-3 (Lines 1–10 of Algorithm 6). Root entry freezes cc and clears xx; demotion enters armed Seek with x=0x=0, bb set to the current local age, and no guard. Birth and replay expiry always enter fresh, and the armed flag persists within a visit.

A root clears old work, scans 1,…,K−11,\ldots,K-1 through BUS/target alternation, and commits at BUS. Demotion after KK consecutive rejected BUS visits has priority over stage completion. Commitment requires both MLM_{L} rounds and an Rc,LR_{c,L}-acceptance suffix within that stage; its entry clears a positive suffix but retains a negative one. The resets are given by StateUpdate (Algorithm 5); the tests are in Lines 12–25 of CollectionFeedback (Algorithm 6).

Work actions and feedback.

Each invocation has indices h=0,…,JL−1h=0,\ldots,J_{L}-1 and starts with S=𝒦S=\mathcal{K}, no held arm or target, and rejection counter z=0z=0. After dLd_{L} parking rounds, WorkAction prioritizes holding, singleton certification, then exploration (Lines 1–8 of Algorithm 7). A held arm persists until deletion. An exploratory target persists until an accepted probe, deletion, or certification, even if it leaves the confidence set. Empty SS disables certification and uses Ca​(𝒦)C_{a}(\mathcal{K}) for exploration without restoring SS.

All exploratory requests satisfy the KK-round cooldown based on acceptances in every mode (Lines 14–18 of Algorithm 7). A filler exists because the preceding K−1K-1 rounds contain at most K−1K-1 acceptances; it cannot be the uncooled target. Only held/probe rejections at hD,L≤h<fLh_{D,L}\leq h<f_{L} extend zz. Target creation, certification, fillers, acceptances, deletion, and rounds outside that window reset zz. At z=Kz=K, the requested arm is deleted and held, target, and zz are cleared, even if SS is already empty (Lines 3–9 of Algorithm 8). Certification remains allowed at h=fLh=f_{L}; work always continues through h=JL−1h=J_{L}-1.

After the final work feedback, let vv be the actual request. Lines 13–19 of Algorithm 8 use the old P,ℓP,\ell to compute

Algorithms 3–8 implement section C.1 using (46). In these algorithms, parameter subscripts LL are omitted: in particular, χ=χL\chi=\chi_{L} and J=JLJ=J_{L}. The registers a,ℓ,qa,\ell,q use local ages, P,LP,L are lengths measured in rounds, and hh counts completed work rounds; ⊥\bot denotes an unset register.

The player loop in Algorithm 4 orders each round’s transitions, request, statistics update, and feedback. StateUpdate initializes the state on entry; CollectionFeedback and WorkFeedback process the current outcome and schedule any resulting transition for the next round. During work, the pair (v,k)(v,k) records both the requested arm and the action type, because probes and fillers have different effects on the target and rejection counter. A/R denotes acceptance or rejection feedback. Figure 2 summarizes the local modes and service states. Lemma 12 establishes the overlap of the work invocations and the common window in (54).

C.3 Collection and Recovery

We first bound the duration of inherited replay, then establish collection, mature handoff, and recovery. These results hold on every execution from the prescribed initialization, including histories affected by statistical errors. Collection and handoff are analyzed on intervals with a fixed population. Physical round indices translate the players’ local ages; the protocol itself uses only local ages. In collection arguments, “higher” refers to the private handle order at BUS\mathrm{BUS}, not to a reward mean.

C.3.1 Scale Envelope and Recovery Constants

The output recurrence bounds the lifetime of an inherited replay, including one based on an incorrect statistical decision. This is the scale bound needed for cold recovery.

Lemma 10 (Scale envelope under the prescribed initialization).

Let a0<a1<⋯a_{0}<a_{1}<\cdots be one player’s actual output ages and PmP_{m} its scale after output mm. Then

HL≤Pm≤HL+⌊am−a02⌋.H_{L}\leq P_{m}\leq H_{L}+\left\lfloor\frac{a_{m}-a_{0}}{2}\right\rfloor. (52)

An output at physical time OO has natural replay deadline at most 3​O/2+HL3O/2+H_{L}. Rejections only shorten replay, without allowing collection before local age ℓ+HL\ell+H_{L}.

Proof.

Initially P0=HLP_{0}=H_{L}. Set Xm=Pm−HLX_{m}=P_{m}-H_{L} and δm=am−am−1\delta_{m}=a_{m}-a_{m-1}. Equation (50) gives

Xm=max⁡{Xm−1,⌊3​Xm−1+2​δm4⌋},0≤Xm−Xm−1≤⌊δm2⌋.X_{m}=\max\left\{X_{m-1},\left\lfloor\frac{3X_{m-1}+2\delta_{m}}{4}\right\rfloor\right\},\qquad 0\leq X_{m}-X_{m-1}\leq\left\lfloor\frac{\delta_{m}}{2}\right\rfloor.

O+HL+⌊O−O02⌋≤32​O+HL.O+H_{L}+\left\lfloor\frac{O-O_{0}}{2}\right\rfloor\leq\frac{3}{2}O+H_{L}.
